title: Models, Secure Design Principles & Frameworks
description: Enterprise security architectures and security models, the secure design principles used to build systems, and the main security control frameworks.

nodes.title: Models
nodes.description:
Models are conceptual representations of things. They shrink something down and simplify it, so a complex system can be broken into its components.
Once you understand the components, you can protect each one, and so build security into every part of even a highly complex system.
Some models focus only on confidentiality, some only on integrity, and some on preventing conflicts of interest.

children.title: Enterprise Security Architecture
children.description:
Models that cover the entire enterprise.
- Architecture: a set of components that work together.
- Security architecture: how each component of the architecture is protected.
- Enterprise security architecture: how all the components of the enterprise are protected: people, processes, systems, networks and so on.
Know the three major ones: Zachman, SABSA and TOGAF.

children.title: Zachman
children.description:
An enterprise security architecture. It defines a two-dimensional table that gives a structured way to define an enterprise and break it down into components.
The columns are what, how, where, who, when and why.
You do not need to memorize the table. Just know that Zachman is an enterprise security architecture.

children.title: Sabsa
children.description:
Developed independently of Zachman, but with a very similar layered structure.
Its main characteristic: a risk-driven enterprise security architecture, derived from an analysis of the business requirements for security.
You do not need to memorize its specifics.

children.title: TOGAF
children.description:
The third major enterprise architecture framework.
Its core is the Architecture Development Method (ADM): an iterative cycle to develop and manage an enterprise architecture.
It breaks an organization down into components so that security can be built into each one.
Full name: The Open Group Architecture Framework.

children.title: Security Models
children.description: Models with rules that protect information. There are two major groups: lattice based and rule based.

children.title: Lattice Based
children.description: Models that define ordered layers (levels) of confidentiality or integrity, and what a subject can read or write between the layers.

children.title: Bell-LaPadula
children.description:
A confidentiality-only lattice model.
It defines layers from lower to higher secrecy, and rules for what a subject (a person or a process) can do between the layers.
In short: read down, write up, and read and write only at your own level.

children.title: Confidentiality
children.description:
Bell-LaPadula's single goal: keep information secret from subjects who are not cleared to see it.
It does nothing to protect integrity or availability.

children.title: Simple Security Property
children.description: To maintain confidentiality, you can only read at your own level and below. You can only read down.

children.title: Star Property
children.description: To maintain confidentiality, you can only write at your own level and above. You can only write up.

children.title: Strong Star Property
children.description: If you both read and write, you can only do so at your own level.

children.title: Biba
children.description:
The second lattice-based model. It defines layers of integrity, and rules for what a subject can do between the layers to maintain integrity.
Biba is the mirror image (inverse) of Bell-LaPadula: read up, write down.
There is a third rule, the Invocation Property, but you do not need to know it.

children.title: Integrity
children.description:
Biba is all about _____. Memory trick: think of the I in Biba as _____.
Its layers are levels of _____: low, medium and high.

children.title: Simple Integrity Property
children.description:
To maintain integrity, you can only read at your own level or above. You can only read up.
Reading down would mean reading less meaningful or accurate data.

children.title: Star Integrity Property
children.description:
To maintain integrity, you can only write at your own level or below. You can only write down.
Writing up would corrupt more accurate data.
It is the inverse of the Bell-LaPadula star property.

children.title: Lipner Implementation
children.description:
Not a model itself, but a way to put two models into practice together.
Bell-LaPadula and Biba are inverses of each other. This approach combines them, so a system can maintain both confidentiality and integrity.

children.title: Rule Based
children.description:
The second group of security models: not built on layers of classification.
Know Clark-Wilson and Brewer-Nash. Just recognize Graham-Denning and Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman as members of this group.

children.title: Clark-Wilson
children.description:
A rule-based model that, like Biba, is all about integrity, but goes a lot deeper.
It defines three goals of integrity, and three rules to achieve them.

children.title: 3 goals of integrity
children.description:
1. Prevent unauthorized subjects from making any changes.
2. Prevent authorized subjects from making bad changes.
3. Maintain the consistency of the system.

children.title: 3 Clark-Wilson rules
children.description:
The three rules that achieve the three goals of integrity:
1. Well-formed transactions.
2. Separation of duties.
3. The access triple: subject, program and object.

children.title: Brewer-Nash
children.description: Also known as the Chinese Wall model.

children.title: Prevent conflicts of interest
children.description: Brewer-Nash has one goal: to prevent conflicts of interest.

children.title: Graham-Denning
children.description:
Specifies a set of basic protection rules for how subjects and objects are securely created and deleted, and how access rights are granted, transferred and deleted.
Just recognize it as a rule-based model.

children.title: Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman
children.description:
An enhancement of the Graham-Denning model that adds generic rights.
Just recognize it as a rule-based model.

nodes.title: Secure Design Principles
nodes.description:
Principles that help to securely design, implement and operate systems.
The first six are covered in more detail in other mind maps.

children.title: Threat Modeling
children.description:
A systematic process to identify, enumerate and prioritize the threats to a system, so that all the relevant threats are found.
The threat modeling frameworks to know are covered in the Risk Management mind map in Domain 1.

children.title: Least Privilege
children.description: Restrict a user's actions to only those required to perform their role.

children.title: Defense in Depth
children.description:
Multiple layers of security controls. If one layer fails, or an attacker gets through it, more layers still protect the asset.
Ideally each layer has a complete control: a combination of preventive, detective and corrective controls.

children.title: Secure Defaults
children.description:
Out of the box, a system should come configured with the most secure settings possible.
Example: a new firewall should block all traffic until someone configures it.

children.title: Fail Securely
children.description:
When a system breaks down or crashes, it should end up in a more protected state, not a less protected one.
Example: a firewall that crashes should block all traffic. The opposite is a firewall that lets all traffic through when it crashes.

children.title: Separation of Duties (SoD)
children.description:
A task needs more than one person to complete, to prevent errors and fraud.
With _____ in place, fraud requires collusion.

children.title: Keep it Simple
children.description:
Also called economy of mechanism.
Vulnerabilities inevitably increase as complexity increases. Smaller, less complex systems have fewer vulnerabilities and are easier to test.

children.title: Zero Trust
children.description:
Do not automatically trust anything inside or outside the organization's perimeter. Verify anything and everything that tries to connect to or access the organization's assets.
Being on the internal network earns no trust by itself.

children.title: Trust But Verify
children.description:
Sounds like Zero Trust, but has a different focus: you cannot prevent every attack, so do not focus only on prevention.
Use complete controls: prevention, detection and correction. Put preventive controls in place, but assume they will fail, so also have good detection and response controls.

children.title: Privacy by Design
children.description:
Bake the protection of personal data in from the very start, just as you bake security in. Building controls in from the start is always easier, cheaper and more effective than adding them later.
It is a framework of seven foundational principles, for example:
- Proactive not reactive: do not wait for a breach of personal data before you think about controls to protect it.
- Protection of personal data as the default setting.

children.title: Shared Responsibility
children.description:
Almost every organization relies heavily on service providers, such as cloud service providers. An organization cannot be secure if its service providers do not have good security controls.
So it must be clearly defined who is accountable for what and who does what, and each service provider must clearly understand its part.

nodes.title: Security Frameworks
nodes.description:
Structured sets of standards, controls and best practices that an organization can adopt to build and run its security program.
Know ISO 27001 fairly well. For the others, you do not need to be an expert: know what each one focuses on and is used for.

children.title: ISO 27001
children.description:
The most widely used security framework in the world.
Defines the requirements for an ISMS (Information Security Management System).
In the 2013 version, Annex A defines 114 controls across 14 categories: the best practices for a well-run security program, from security governance and policies through onboarding, asset management, access control, cryptography, physical security and network security, to a compliance function. The 2022 version regroups them into 93 controls in 4 themes.
It defines the controls, so an organization can be ISO 27001 certified.

children.title: ISO 27002
children.description:
The code of practice for information security controls: implementation guidance for the controls in ISO 27001.
It is only a guidance document, so you cannot be certified against it.

children.title: NIST 800-53
children.description: A detailed catalog of security and privacy controls, organized into control families, for US federal agencies and their information systems.

children.title: COBIT
children.description:
A framework for IT governance and management.
Created by the IT auditors at ISACA, so it is particularly useful for audit and assurance work.

children.title: ITIL
children.description:
A framework of best practices for IT service management: delivering IT services that are aligned with business goals and objectives.
Particularly useful for IT processes such as change management, configuration management, access management, event management and availability management.
Full name: Information Technology Infrastructure Library.

children.title: HIPAA
children.description:
A US federal law focused on safeguarding medical information.
Full name: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act.

children.title: SOX
children.description:
A US federal law that followed the Enron and WorldCom scandals.
Top management must individually certify that financial information is accurate, and the penalties for fraudulent activity are much more severe.
The security aspect: financial records must have integrity and be available.

children.title: FedRAMP
children.description:
A standardized approach to security assessment, authorization and continuous monitoring for cloud products and services.
Any cloud service used by a US federal government entity must be FedRAMP approved.

children.title: FISMA
children.description:
A US federal law that defines security requirements for US federal government agencies and contractors.
Each agency must develop, document and implement an agency-wide information security program.

children.title: Cyber Kill Chain
children.description:
Defines seven stages of common cyberattacks: the points where the security team can prevent, detect or intercept attackers.
Stop the attack at any one stage and there is no attack. The earlier you stop it, the less chance the attack harms the organization.
Know the order of the seven stages and, at a high level, what happens at each:
1. Reconnaissance
2. Weaponization
3. Delivery
4. Exploit
5. Installation
6. Command & Control
7. Actions
